ch14.title: The Seventy and the Camp at Pella
ch14.b002: On Thursday morning, August 18, nearly a hundred evangelists and disciples were waiting at Magadan Park, the women’s corps among them. The Master called them together and gave his orders. Each apostle was to take one of the twelve evangelists as his partner, and the remaining evangelists were to be divided among them, so that twelve groups would go out to labor in the cities and villages of the Decapolis. The women’s corps and some of the other disciples would stay with him. The tour would last four weeks. They were to be back at Magadan no later than Friday, September 16, and in the meantime he promised to visit them often.
ch14.b003: Judas Iscariot spent the morning dividing the purse. He worked out what each of the twelve groups would need and counted it into twelve small bags. Most of it was money that David’s messengers had gathered and brought in. He counted without a smile. Four weeks would be tight. And he thought he already knew what this tour would bring. The crowds would not come. There would be no signs. He was right. The groups went to Gerasa and Gamala, to Hippos and Gadara, to Abila and Edrei, to Philadelphia and Heshbon and Scythopolis and a dozen other towns, and in the whole of that month no one was healed by a miracle, and nothing else out of the ordinary happened anywhere.
ch14.b004: Judas found it hard to bear. He missed the crowds. He missed the day when five thousand had sat down on the grass, the noise and the heat of it, the evening when the people had stirred and murmured and tried to make the Master king. On that day he had felt that he stood at the center of something enormous. Now he stood in the dim yard of a small village, talking to ten people, twenty at most. The foot of Hermon was still in his chest as well: the scribes laughing, the boy in his fit, and afterward the rebuke in the garden of Celsus, that their motives had not been pure. Judas had turned the words over many times. It was he and Simon Zelotes who had stepped forward to heal the boy, and yet the rebuke had fallen on all nine of them alike. He found that a little unfair, and also a little comforting.
ch14.b005: The Master kept his promise and went from group to group. At Hippos, where Simon Peter was in charge, he taught one evening about forgiveness. Peter asked him how often he had to forgive a brother who wronged him. Would seven times be enough? Not seven, the Master said, but seventy times and seven. Then he told the story of a king’s chief steward who owed his lord ten thousand talents and was forgiven the whole of it, and who went out and found a fellow steward who owed him a mere hundred denarii, and took him by the throat. At Gamala he visited John Zebedee. John told him that the day before he had gone over to Ashtaroth and found a man teaching in the Master’s name and even claiming to cast out devils, and since the fellow had never been one of them, John had forbidden him. The Master told him not to forbid such men. It would be better, he said, to count anyone who was not against them as being for them. John was badly confused. It was a lesson he would come back to again and again in later years.
ch14.b006: Judas heard these stories secondhand, from men in the other groups. He worked out the hundred denarii against the ten thousand talents. How many times over was the one debt the other? He finished the sum quickly. The gap was so large that the story stopped feeling real. Who was ever forgiven a debt like that? He tried to think whether he had ever owed anyone so much. Nothing came to mind. He had always paid exactly what he owed. He was a man who neither ran up debts nor needed them forgiven, and that was the thing about himself he had always been proudest of.
ch14.b008: At Edrei, where Thomas and his partners were working, the Master stayed a day and a night. In the evening he spoke about the principles that ought to guide anyone who carried the truth to others. Always respect a man’s personality, he told them. A righteous cause must never be pushed forward by force, and that meant the force of the mind as much as the force of the hand. They were not to bring people into the kingdom by crushing arguments or by a show of mental superiority, nor to flatten a person’s mind under the sheer weight of logic.
ch14.b009: Thomas listened with his ears burning. Winning arguments was what he did best, and in his weeks at Edrei he had done it more than once. In the synagogue yard he had cornered a teacher of the law point by point until the man had no reply left, and he had gone away pleased with himself. The man had never come back. Now Thomas thought he understood why. He had won the argument and lost the man. The Master went on. They were not to tear down people’s self-respect, he said. Instead of fixing only on what was wrong in a person’s life, they should be generous in noticing what deserved praise. Thomas smiled crookedly to himself. Praise was the thing he was worst at, after Andrew.
ch14.b010: From Edrei the Master went on to Abila, where Nathaniel and his partners were laboring. Nathaniel had been troubled for some time. Certain things the Master said seemed to him to chip away at the authority of the Hebrew scriptures. He had grown up in Cana learning that the Scriptures were the word of God. The rabbis taught that the words of the law had been with God in heaven before ever Abraham or Moses lived. Yet whenever the Master taught from the Scriptures, he chose only certain parts. The best parts, as Nathaniel saw it.
ch14.b011: That night, when the usual hour of questions and answers was over, Nathaniel drew the Master away from the others. They stood under an olive tree at the edge of the village. He hesitated, then asked whether the Master would trust him with the truth about the Scriptures. He had noticed, he said, that the Master taught only a portion of them, and he took it that the Master did not accept what the rabbis said. What, then, was the truth?
ch14.b012: The Master told him he had judged rightly. He did not look on the Scriptures as the rabbis did. But Nathaniel was not to pass this on to his brothers, who were not all ready for it. Then he explained. The law of Moses and the writings of the Scriptures had not existed before Abraham. They had been gathered together, in the form they now had, only in fairly recent times. They held the best of the higher thoughts and longings of the Jewish people, but they also held a great deal that did not truly show the character of the Father in heaven. They were the work of men, some of them holy and some of them not. And yet Nathaniel was not to mistake him: for all that, they were the finest collection of religious wisdom and spiritual truth to be found anywhere in the world at that time.
ch14.b013: Nathaniel must never believe, the Master said, those records that told how the God of love had sent his fathers out to kill their enemies, men and women and children alike. Those were the words of men, and not very holy men. The Scriptures always mirrored the mind and morals and spiritual standing of the people who wrote them. Had he not noticed how the picture of God grew more beautiful and glorious as the prophets wrote, from Samuel down to Isaiah? Nothing that human nature had touched could be held infallible. Divine truth could truly shine through a man’s mind, but always with only a relative purity. Only the Creators possessed infallibility.
ch14.b014: Nathaniel put his hand against the trunk of the olive tree. His legs were unsteady. His eyes had been opened, and at the same moment he felt as if he had been struck. A corner of the floor he had stood on since childhood had fallen away. And yet, strangely, he did not fall. Under the place that had broken there was something firmer. The authority of truth, the Master had said, lived in the spirit that dwelt in truth’s living expressions, not in the dead words of men of another age. Nathaniel thought: until now I have believed in a book. From now on I must believe in the longing that made men write it, the longing of people who were searching for God. And in this man, who had come to answer that longing.
ch14.b015: The Master added one thing more. The reason they made no written record of the gospel now, he said, was that after he had gone they might read such records in different ways and split into quarreling parties over the truth. For this generation it was best to live these truths and leave the writing alone.
ch14.b016: Nathaniel carried that conversation deep in his soul for a long time. He told none of his brothers about it until after the Master had ascended, and even then he never found the courage to tell the whole of it. That night he went back to his sleeping mat and lay awake a long while. When the evangelist sleeping beside him asked what was the matter, he only said:
ch14.b017: “Nothing at all. I was wondering whether Jonah was ever really inside the whale.”
ch14.b018: The evangelist laughed and rolled over. Nathaniel did not laugh. The Master had told him that even if Jonah had never lived, the truth of that story, God’s love for the people of Nineveh whom the Jews called heathen, would lose none of its worth. Nathaniel held on to that and fell asleep. On the broken floor, for the first time, he slept in peace.
ch14.b020: On September 16 the twelve groups came back to Magadan. Hundreds of souls had entered the kingdom in the Decapolis. Without wonders, and without the Master at their side, they had done it. On Sunday morning, September 18, Andrew announced that there would be no work in the coming week. The apostles went home to visit their families. Only Nathaniel and Thomas stayed behind.
ch14.b021: A Greek philosopher had come from Alexandria. His name was Rodan, and he had become a disciple of Jesus through the teaching of one of Abner’s associates who had led a mission in Alexandria. He wanted to bring his whole philosophy of life into harmony with Jesus’ teaching, and he had come hoping the Master would talk it through with him. The Master received him warmly but would not enter the discussion himself. Instead he told Nathaniel and Thomas to hear out everything Rodan had to say and to tell him about the gospel in return.
ch14.b022: The two looked at each other. Nathaniel was, with Judas, one of the two best educated men among the twelve. Thomas had the one truly analytical mind in the group. But neither of them had ever sat across from a Greek philosopher. Early on Monday morning Rodan began a series of ten addresses to Nathaniel, Thomas and about two dozen believers who happened to be at Magadan. And through that week the two apostles took turns telling him about the gospel of the kingdom.
ch14.b023: On Sunday, September 25, the apostles and evangelists gathered again at Magadan. That evening the Master surprised everyone by announcing that early the next morning he and the twelve would set out for Jerusalem to attend the feast of tabernacles. Nathaniel and Thomas were still in the middle of their talks with Rodan, and they asked leave to stay a few more days. The Master gave it.
ch14.b024: The one point on which Rodan and the two apostles could not agree was the personality of God. Rodan readily accepted everything they said about God’s attributes. But the Father in heaven, he insisted, could not be a person in the way men understood personality. Personality, he argued, consisted in full and mutual communication between beings who were equals. No one was God’s equal. And so God stood above personality, as the Creator stands above the creature.
ch14.b025: Thomas ran into that argument as into a wall. He tapped at every joint of it and could find no crack. Thomas argued that God did communicate with man; Rodan replied that God had never shown himself personally and remained a mystery. Nathaniel appealed to his own experience of God, and Rodan granted it but said that such experience proved only that God was real, not that he was a person. The two apostles asked the Master for help. He would not enter the debate. He only told Thomas that it mattered little what idea of the Father he held, so long as he knew in spirit the ideal of the Father’s infinite and eternal nature.
ch14.b026: At first Thomas was hurt. He will not help us, he thought. By Monday night he had given up the argument altogether. But lying awake that night and turning the Master’s words over, he began to hear something else in them. Winning the argument was not what mattered. It was the same thread that had run through what he had heard at Edrei. The next day Thomas did not try to beat Rodan. He sat with him and thought alongside him, and let Nathaniel carry the reasoning. And strangely, a way opened. The apostles had found it hard to prove that God was a person, but Rodan found it harder still to prove that he was not. By Tuesday night Nathaniel had won him over. Rodan said that he would confess God as a person, provided he might add to the meaning of personality a whole range of values beyond the human, the infinite, the eternal and the universal. God, he said, must be infinitely more than a person, but he could not be anything less. And he accepted Jesus as the personal revelation of the Father.
ch14.b027: One matter remained: the divinity of Jesus, a teaching the Master had only lately begun to declare openly. Nathaniel and Thomas worked it out together and set it before Rodan. It was the first time either of them had tried to explain it in his own words, out of his own mouth.
ch14.b028: Nathaniel began. The Master had admitted his divinity, he said, and they believed him. Much that had happened around him could be understood only by believing that he was the Son of God as well as the Son of Man. Thomas took it up. Their life with him showed what human friendship was meant to be, and only a divine being could be such a human friend. He was the most unselfish man they had ever known. He was a friend even to sinners, and he dared to love his enemies. He did not hesitate to rebuke them, but it was plain to everyone that he loved them.
ch14.b029: Thomas’s voice caught as he said it. He does not hesitate to rebuke us, but he plainly loves us. He was thinking of the night they had come back from the foot of Hermon, of the rebuke about impure motives, and of the face of the one who had spoken it. That face had not been angry. It had been in pain. Thomas stopped speaking in front of Rodan. Nathaniel touched him lightly on the back and went on for him. The better Rodan came to know him, the more he would love him. They knew he was a man; they were certain of that. But they were almost as certain that he was divine.
ch14.b030: Rodan was silent for a long time. Then he bowed his head to them, a philosopher bowing to two men from Galilee. The pair set off in haste, hoping to reach Jerusalem by Friday. On the road Nathaniel said:
ch14.b032: “No,” said Thomas. “We spoke. For the first time.”
ch14.b033: Rodan went back to Alexandria and for many years taught his philosophy in the school of Meganta. He remained a faithful believer to the end, and he gave up his life in Greece when the persecutions were at their worst.
ch14.b034: Boldness at the Feast of Tabernacles
ch14.b035: Meanwhile the Master and the ten were making for Jerusalem by way of Samaria. Near nightfall the Master sent Philip and Matthew to a village on the eastern slopes of Mount Gilboa to find lodging. The people there hated Jews even more than most Samaritans did, and with so many pilgrims passing through on the way to the feast of tabernacles, the feeling was sharper than usual. They refused lodging because the travelers were Jews, and when Philip and Matthew protested, the villagers drove them out with sticks and stones. When the two came back, James and John stepped up to the Master and asked his permission to call down fire from heaven to consume those people. The Master turned on the sons of Zebedee and rebuked them sternly. They did not know what kind of spirit they were showing, he said; vengeance had no place in the kingdom of heaven. Rather than quarrel, they would go on to the little village by the Jordan ford.
ch14.b036: Judas Iscariot watched the scene from behind. Fire from heaven. He laughed inwardly. The sons of Zebedee could say a thing like that; they were always at the Master’s side. But another thought followed. What if the Master really did call down fire? What if, just once, he let that power be seen? Judas put the thought away quickly. The Master always drew back. He had drawn back this time too.
ch14.b037: Late on Wednesday evening they reached Bethany, having come the rest of the way by the east Jordan road. And from the next day on, things happened that no one had expected. The Master went into Jerusalem and began to teach openly in the temple. The apostles were stunned. They knew the Sanhedrin wanted to bring him to trial. They remembered how often lately he had spoken of his death. For a long time they had begged him to proclaim the gospel in Jerusalem, and now that he was doing it they tried to hold him back. It made no difference. Several times he taught in Solomon’s Porch and in the temple courts, and thousands of pilgrims from every part of the Roman Empire saw him and heard him.
ch14.b038: Judas stood in the shade of a pillar in the temple court and watched him, and something twisted inside him. Some months before, he had dared to think that the Master had fled in haste into Phoenicia because he was afraid of the Jewish leaders and of Herod Antipas. He had never said it aloud, but he had written it down plainly in the ledger he kept in his heart. And now here was the same man, under the very nose of the Sanhedrin, in the middle of those who wanted him dead, speaking without the least hesitation. All the whispers about fear and cowardice ended for good that week.
ch14.b039: Judas had to strike out a line in his ledger. It did not please him. It made him angry, and he could not tell at what. At having been wrong, perhaps. But if it had not been fear, why had they fled? Why had they abandoned Capernaum and wandered the gentile coast? A man who was not afraid and still would not use his power: that was harder to understand than fear. Judas did not follow the question to its end. He had a dim sense of what he would find there, that the kingdom he wanted and the kingdom this man meant to build were not the same. He did not want to look at that. So he closed the ledger, and on another line he wrote: one more thing that does not add up.
ch14.b040: On Friday Nathaniel and Thomas arrived. They told the story of Rodan, and the other apostles learned a great deal from it. After the feast the Master divided his time between Bethany and Bethlehem. At Bethlehem he taught Abner and the other former apostles of John the Baptist, and at last they gave themselves wholeheartedly to the kingdom. It was agreed that they would soon join the Master at Magadan Park. Late in October the Master and the twelve withdrew. On Sunday, October 30, after a few days’ rest at Ephraim, they took the west Jordan highway straight to Magadan Park and arrived there on Wednesday, November 2. The apostles were greatly relieved to be on friendly ground again. They no longer urged him to go up to Jerusalem.
ch14.b042: A few days later Abner arrived from Bethlehem with about fifty disciples. Gathered at the Magadan camp now were the evangelistic corps, the women’s corps, and about a hundred and fifty proven disciples from every part of Palestine. On Friday, November 4, an intensive course of training began for them. The Master spoke to them every morning. Peter taught methods of public preaching; Nathaniel taught the art of teaching; Thomas explained how to answer questions; Matthew showed them how to organize the finances of their groups. The other apostles helped as their own experience and gifts allowed.
ch14.b043: When Thomas taught them how to answer questions, he told them about Edrei. Do not beat a man down with argument, he said. Most people who ask a question want respect before they want an answer. The disciples wrote it down. Thomas listened to himself saying it and was a little surprised. Three months earlier he would never have said such a thing.
ch14.b044: On the Sabbath, November 19, at about two in the afternoon, between showers of rain, David arrived with most of his messenger corps. More than four hundred believers gathered on the shore of the lake of Galilee to witness the ordination of the seventy: Abner and ten of John’s former apostles, fifty-one of the early evangelists, and eight other disciples who had distinguished themselves in the work of the kingdom.
ch14.b045: The Master spoke to them first. The harvest was great, he said, and the laborers few, so they should pray the Lord of the harvest to send still more. He was sending them out like lambs among wolves. They were to go two by two and carry neither purse nor extra clothing. In whatever house they stayed, they were first to wish peace on that household. They were to eat and drink what was set before them and not move from house to house looking for better lodging. They must be wise as serpents and harmless as doves. They had received the good things of the kingdom freely, and freely they should give.
ch14.b046: Then the seventy knelt in a circle around him, and beginning with Abner, he laid his hands on the head of every man.
ch14.b047: The Alpheus twins went back and forth along the edge of the crowd of four hundred, seating people so that they would not press forward. Both their faces were wet with rain, and both were smiling in exactly the same way. Judas Iscariot stood at the edge of the gathering and watched the hands being laid on. There was a smell of wet grass. A drop of rain fell on his forehead. He remembered: almost three years earlier, on the highland north of Capernaum, the cold of the winter ground. On that day the first head the Master’s hands had rested on was his. A carpenter’s hands, broad-knuckled and warm. While they rested on his head, all the counting inside him had stopped for a moment. He had not forgotten it. He could not forget it.
ch14.b048: And now the same hands rested on Abner’s head. Then on the next man’s, and the next. Seventy times. Judas counted. Those hands had now been laid not on twelve heads but on eighty-two. For a long time he had wondered what it meant that he had been first. An honor? Or a worry? Today he felt the question grow strangely small. First or seventieth, the hands were the same hands. That ought to have comforted him. It did not. He read it this way instead: we are only a few among many. The specialness he had been clinging to seemed to be washing away in the rain.
ch14.b049: Nathaniel was standing next to Judas. He saw that Judas’s face had gone hard, and he could not guess what he was thinking. Of all the twelve, Judas was the only one Nathaniel did not get along with. He did not know that Judas had once gone secretly to the Master to complain that he did not take his apostleship seriously enough. He knew only that Judas had never once laughed at any of his jokes. Still, that day, he spoke to him.
ch14.b050: “It didn’t rain on us, as I remember.”
ch14.b051: Judas looked at him. Then he laughed, very briefly. It was the first time Nathaniel had ever seen him laugh. The laugh was gone almost at once.
ch14.b052: Early the next morning Abner sent the seventy messengers out into all the cities of Galilee, Samaria and Judea, thirty-five pairs of them. They would preach and teach for about six weeks and then return to the new camp near Pella, in Perea, on Friday, December 30.
ch14.b054: More than fifty disciples who had hoped to be among the seventy were not chosen. The candidates had been weighed by a committee of three: Andrew, Abner, and the acting head of the evangelistic corps. Whenever the three could not agree, they brought the candidate to the Master, and the Master never turned away a single man who longed to be ordained. But more than a dozen of them, after they had talked with him, no longer wished to go.
ch14.b055: About that time Andrew brought a rich young man to the Master. His name was Matadormus, and he was a member of the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem. He had heard the Master teach and had afterward been instructed in the gospel by Peter and the other apostles, and he wanted to be ordained. The Master talked with him about what ordination required and asked him to think it over before deciding. Early the next morning, as the Master was out walking, the young man stopped him. He had kept all the commandments since he was a boy, he said. What more must he do to gain eternal life? The Master told him that keeping the commandments was good, but that salvation was the reward of faith, not merely of works. Did he believe the gospel of the kingdom? He said he did. Then, the Master told him, he was truly his disciple and a child of the kingdom.
ch14.b056: But the young man was not content to be a disciple. He wanted to be one of the new messengers. The Master looked down at him with great love and said that he would have him as a messenger, if he was willing to pay the price and to supply the one thing he lacked. The young man said he would do anything. The Master kissed him on the forehead as he knelt and told him to go and sell everything he owned, give the money to the poor or to his brethren, and then come and follow him; he would have treasure in the kingdom of heaven. The young man’s face fell. He stood up and went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.
ch14.b057: Judas watched from a little way off. He followed the hem of the Sanhedrin member’s fine robe as it trailed through the Magadan mud and moved away. What a waste, he thought. If only wealth like that had come into the kingdom’s treasury. Judas was not ashamed of thinking so. That was his work. He was the treasurer of the twelve, the man who had smiled bitterly at Caesarea-Philippi holding up an empty purse. He thought: if that young man had given up his wealth, it might well have been put back into his own hands to manage, as treasurer of the seventy. The Master did that kind of thing. Then he stopped. In that case, why had he gone away? What he gave up might have come back to him.
ch14.b058: Judas knew the answer. It was not the wealth the Master wanted. It was to free the man from loving it. Nearly everyone has one thing he holds on to and cherishes, and the kingdom asks for that thing as the price of admission. Judas understood that. He understood it too well, and it made him uneasy. He tried to think what his own one thing might be. Not money. He was honest about money. Then what? He turned his mind away before he found the answer. Looking into himself was the thing he did worst. No: it was the thing he most avoided.
ch14.b059: Two Men at the Feast of Dedication
ch14.b060: The last ten days of November were spent in council at Magadan. At daybreak on Tuesday, December 6, the whole company of almost three hundred set out with all their belongings, and that night they lodged by the river near Pella, close to where the Master had been baptized in the Jordan. It was the very place, by the spring, where John the Baptist had made his camp some years before. Soon afterward David Zebedee came down the Jordan with his messengers and pack animals loaded with camp equipment, and about half a mile north of the apostles he set up a camp that could take in nearly fifteen hundred visitors. It was the rainy season. Winter rain fell on the tents.
ch14.b061: While the camp at Pella was being set up, the Master took Nathaniel and Thomas and went secretly up to Jerusalem for the feast of the dedication. Not until they had crossed the Jordan at the Bethany ford did the two realize that he meant to go on to Jerusalem. They pleaded with him earnestly and used every argument they could think of. It was folly, they said, and dangerous, to put himself in the hands of the Sanhedrin. More than once Thomas stopped in the road and turned to face him and argued again. The Master answered only that he wanted to give the teachers of Israel one more chance to see the light before his hour came.
ch14.b062: Thomas gave way. And then he walked on. He was a man who argued against a thing to the end, and once it was decided, was the first to move. He grumbled to Nathaniel:
ch14.b063: “He always picks the most dangerous road.”
ch14.b064: “And you always walk it at the front.”
ch14.b065: Thomas had no answer to that. They spent the night at Jericho. On Friday night, at the house of Nicodemus, the Master met some twenty-five Jewish leaders who believed his teaching, fourteen of them present or former members of the Sanhedrin; Matadormus was among them. They offered to go with him before the council. The Master told them it would do no good; they would only bring more anger down on their own heads. Each of them should go about the Father’s business as the spirit led him. That night, on the Mount of Olives, Nathaniel and Thomas hardly slept.
ch14.b066: The next morning, the Sabbath, the three of them had breakfast at Martha’s house in Bethany and then went into Jerusalem. As they came near the temple they passed a beggar who had been born blind, sitting in his usual place. The Master stopped and looked at him. Nathaniel asked whose sin had caused the man to be born blind, his own or his parents’. That was what the rabbis taught. Nathaniel had grown up being taught it too. Since the night at Abila, he had been taking such teachings out one by one and looking at them again.
ch14.b067: The Master told him that neither the man nor his parents had sinned. The blindness had come in the natural course of events. But they must do the work of the one who had sent him while it was still day, for night was coming when it could not be done. And on this Sabbath, he said, they would give the man his sight, and so hand the scribes and Pharisees the very occasion they were looking for. He spat on the ground and made clay, put it on the man’s eyes, and told him to go and wash in the pool of Siloam. The beggar, whose name was Josiah, did as he was told, and came back seeing.
ch14.b068: That afternoon the leaders of the Sanhedrin broke their own rule against meeting on the Sabbath and called the council together. But they did not call the Master. They were afraid to. Instead they sent for Josiah, questioned him, and in the end had him cast out of the synagogue. Nathaniel and Thomas were present at the session. Thomas heard Josiah answer. The man knew very little. He knew a man called Jesus had healed him, but not who that man truly was. He simply told what had happened to him: the man had put clay on his eyes and told him to wash, and now he could see. However hard the council pressed him, he would not be moved from that.
ch14.b069: Only after they heard that Josiah had been cast out did the Master and the two apostles go looking for him at his home. Thomas called him out into the yard. It was a winter evening, and rainwater dripped from the edge of the roof. Josiah came out blinking. His eyes were not yet used to the light. The Master asked him whether he believed in the Son of God. Josiah said that if he were told who that was, he would believe. The Master told him that he had both seen him and heard him; it was he who was speaking to him now.
ch14.b070: Josiah fell down where he stood. Lord, I believe, he said, and he worshiped him.
ch14.b071: Thomas stood in a corner of the yard and watched. He could not breathe. This man had not asked for proof. No: this man had already been given proof. Eyes closed since birth had been opened. And still he had not carried that proof back to argue over it. He had asked who had healed him, and the moment he was told, he was on his knees. Thomas wondered what he himself would have done. He would have opened his eyes and doubted them. Was he really seeing? And what was he seeing? He watched Josiah’s rain-soaked back for a long time. He envied a man who could kneel like that. And he was a little afraid: that one day he too might have to kneel like that. When that day would come, or before what, he did not know.
ch14.b072: Nathaniel tugged at his sleeve. It was time to go. Josiah went with them; the Master had told him to make ready to come to the camp at Pella. All the way back Thomas said not a word. Nathaniel made no jokes either.
ch14.b074: On Friday, December 30, while the Master was up in the nearby hills with Peter, James and John, the seventy came back to Pella in pairs, bringing many believers with them. When the Master returned at about five o’clock, all seventy were gathered at the teaching place. Supper was put off for more than an hour while they poured out what they had seen. Much of their news had already reached the camp through David’s messengers, but it was something else to hear the newly ordained teachers tell in their own words how hungry Jews and gentiles had received their message.
ch14.b075: They said that even the devils had been subject to them. At that Nathaniel remembered the foot of Hermon: the boy in his fit, the words of command from Simon Zelotes that came to nothing, the scribes laughing. What nine apostles had not been able to do a few months before, these seventy were saying they had done. Nathaniel was not ashamed. He was glad. And he was amused. Heaven was always one step ahead of them.
ch14.b076: The Master rejoiced with them. He had seen Satan fall like lightning from heaven, he said. But they were not to rejoice too much over this; they should rejoice rather that their names were written in heaven. And then, just before the evening meal, he had one of those rare moments of overflowing joy that his followers had seen now and then. He thanked his Father that this wonderful gospel had been hidden from the wise and the self-righteous and shown to these children of the kingdom. He was glad, he said, to know that the good news would spread through all the world even after he had gone back to the Father.
ch14.b077: Thomas watched the Master’s face as he prayed. He had seen that face only a few times before. The calm he knew so well was brimming over with joy. Suddenly Thomas understood. This man was getting ready to leave. He was glad because he saw that the work could go on without him. Thomas did not know whether to share that gladness or to grieve over what it meant. He did both.
ch14.b078: Then the Master turned to them and said that the eyes which saw these things and the ears which heard them were blessed. Many prophets and great men of earlier ages had longed to see what they were seeing and had not been allowed. The next day, the Sabbath, he took the seventy aside and warned them sternly against pride, spiritual pride. And he told them that anyone who labored and was heavy laden should come to him, and they would find rest for their souls.
ch14.b080: On Tuesday, January 3, A.D. 30, Abner called the seventy together, gave them their final instructions, and sent them out to all the cities and villages of Perea. The mission would last nearly three months; it was the Master’s last. The women’s corps, now sixty-two strong, took over most of the care of the sick. Among them were Perpetua, Peter’s wife, the wives of Philip and Matthew, and the mother of James and John. No miracles were worked on this mission. Yet nowhere else in Palestine did the better sort of citizens so generally accept the Master’s teaching.
ch14.b081: The Master went back and forth between the camp at Pella and the towns where the seventy were working. By the middle of January more than twelve hundred people were gathered at Pella, and by the end of the month the Sabbath-afternoon crowds numbered almost three thousand. When rain did not prevent it, the Master taught them at nine in the morning. Peter and the other apostles taught in the afternoons. In the evenings the twelve and the more advanced disciples sat with him for questions and answers. Through all of those three months at least ten of the apostles were always with him.
ch14.b082: Judas looked at the crowds and breathed more easily. The people had come back. Not as in the Galilean days, but the number three thousand made his heart beat fast again. Yet there were still no signs. The people did not come to see wonders. They came to listen. Judas found that strange. If people would gather without miracles, then what had he been hoping for all this time? He pushed that question into a corner of the ledger too. That corner was getting rather heavy.
ch14.b083: In February the Master and the twelve went round the towns of northern Perea. On the way to Philadelphia, as they ate their noon meal in the shade, Thomas asked whether spirit beings had a hand in the strange things that happened in the world, and whether the angels could prevent accidents. The Master asked whether he had been with him so long and still asked such things. Had they not seen how the Son of Man always refused to use the forces of heaven for his own keeping? The Father sent his rain on the just and the unjust alike. The eighteen men killed when the tower of Siloam fell, he said, had been no worse sinners than anyone else in Jerusalem.
ch14.b084: Thomas stored that answer away. Then he looked at Nathaniel. Nathaniel nodded, a piece of bread still in his mouth. They were thinking the same thing. The man born blind: not his sin, nor his parents’. The fallen tower: not those men’s sin either. The world does not run on God’s rewards and punishments. And still God walks through that world beside them.
ch14.b085: Judas sat a little apart and listened. He does not use the powers of heaven for his own keeping. Judas held on to that for a long time. He remembered the empty treasury, the empty purse he had turned inside out at Caesarea-Philippi. The Master had not lifted a finger then. He had simply waited until David’s messengers brought money. Judas had been calling that timidity. Today the Master called it principle. Judas did not want to know which name was right. He got up and saw to the baggage. There were accounts to settle. Counting always made him feel better.
ch14.b086: On the way back to the spring at Pella, the rain stopped. Beyond the Jordan valley the hills of Judea showed faintly. Beyond those hills lay Jerusalem. Thomas looked that way for a long time. He had heard how, at the feast of the dedication, men in that city had run to pick up stones to throw at the Master. Before long the Master would go there again. Thomas knew it. And he thought he knew what he would say when that day came. He would argue against it, to the very end. And when it was decided, he would be the first to stand up.
ch14.b088: The course of events follows episodes from Papers 159 through 166 that matter most to the apostles: the pairing of apostles and evangelists for the four weeks in the Decapolis and the absence of miracles (159:0.1–0.2); the teaching on forgiveness at Hippos and Peter’s question (159:1.1–1.5); John forbidding the stranger, reported at Gamala (159:2.1–2.3); the principles given at Edrei (159:3.1–3.4); Nathaniel’s private question at Abila, the Master’s answer on the Scriptures, and Nathaniel’s silence until after the ascension (159:4.1–4.11); the return to Magadan (159:6.1–6.2); Rodan and his discussions with Nathaniel and Thomas, the debate on the personality of God, the word to Thomas, the two apostles’ account of Jesus’ divinity, and Rodan’s later life (160:0.1, 160:1.1, 161:0.1–2.12); the refusal at the Samaritan village and the rebuke of the sons of Zebedee (162:0.1–0.3); the open teaching at the feast of tabernacles and Judas’s thought that Jesus had fled from fear (162:1.1–1.9); the union with Abner’s group and the return to Magadan (162:9.1–9.7); the training course and the apostles’ parts in it (163:0.1–0.2); the ordination of the seventy (163:1.1–1.6); the choosing of candidates and Matadormus (163:2.1–2.11); the move to Pella and David’s camp (163:5.1–5.3); the return of the seventy and Jesus’ prayer (163:6.1–6.7); the feast of the dedication with Nathaniel and Thomas, the meeting at Nicodemus’s house, the healing of Josiah, the Sabbath session of the Sanhedrin and Josiah’s confession (164:0.1–5.6); the Perean mission and the women’s corps (163:7.2–7.3, 165:0.1–0.4, 165:1.1, 165:3.1); and Thomas’s question on the road to Philadelphia (166:0.1, 166:4.1–4.4). Character details come from Paper 139: Nathaniel and Judas as the best educated of the twelve and Judas’s complaint against Nathaniel (139:6.2, 6.5), Thomas’s analytical mind and his “Let’s go” (139:8.2, 8.8), Judas’s longing for crowds and his view that Jesus was afraid to assert his power (139:12.4, 157:7.2), and Judas being the first to receive the Master’s hands at the ordination of the twelve (140:2.1).
ch14.b089: Added as fiction are the inner thoughts and memories of Nathaniel, Thomas and Judas; the olive tree, the winter rain and the dripping eaves; Thomas cornering a teacher of the law at Edrei; Nathaniel’s joke about Jonah to the evangelist; the short exchanges between Nathaniel and Thomas on the road; Nathaniel’s remark to Judas at the ordination; Rodan’s bow; the image of the ledger Judas keeps in his heart; and the twins seating the crowd on the day of the ordination. That Judas heard the stories of Hippos and Gamala secondhand, and that he watched the ordination and the Matadormus scene, are also invented. The text says Nathaniel and Thomas presented Jesus’ divinity jointly; dividing their words between them is a narrative device.
ch14.b090: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
